body.text: In a development Fish News is choosing to describe as a scheduling setback, our field correspondent Minivan was pulled from open water by the Royal Navy this week, shortly after his boat stopped being on top of the sea and began being underneath it.

Minivan had been stationed in the area to investigate reports of a mysterious signal affecting the local salmon population. Those reports have since been traced, with some confidence, to the exact stretch of water in which his boat went down. Fish News does not regard this as a coincidence, nor is it prepared to regard it as anything else.
Asked about the incident, Chunce Whatney said only: "The mystery of the signal continues." When pressed on the wellbeing of his colleague, Mr Whatney had already left the room.

Minivan is understood to be in stable condition. Rescuers credit the relatively warm water in the area, which one described as "the only part of this that went to plan." Reports of a shark attack remain unconfirmed. A local fisherman, speaking on condition of anonymity from the deck of a trawler with his full name painted down the side, said he "wouldn't rule it out," adding that he had not been asked about sharks but held strong views on them regardless.

When Fish News approached the Royal Navy for comment, a medic aboard the rescue vessel replied that the matter was "none of your f***ing business," before instructing our correspondent to sit still while an IV was put in.
Footage of the sinking has since come to light. Fish News did not send a camera. No one at Fish News has been able to establish who did, and the salmon have so far declined to comment.
Fish News remains committed to calm, unsensational reporting, and will continue to monitor the situation, along with any response from local authorities, from dry land.
